## Today's Learning Goals

::: {.small-text}
By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

- Perform <span style="color: purple;">likelihood-based model selection</span> through analysis of deviance, Akaike Information Criterion, and Bayesian Information Criterion.
- Extend the link function concept of the generalized linear models (GLMs) to other discrete <span style="color: purple;">categorical responses</span>.
- Outline the modelling framework of the <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial Logistic regression</span>.
- Fit and interpret the Multinomial Logistic regression.
- Use the Multinomial Logistic regression for prediction.
:::

## Outline

1. Likelihood-based Model Selection
2. Categorical Type Responses
3. Multinomial Logistic Regression

## 1. Likelihood-based Model Selection

<br>

- In <span style="color: purple;">DSCI 561</span>, you learned about <span style="color: purple;">model selection</span> in Ordinary Least-squares (OLS) via Mallow’s $C_p$, Akaike information criterion (AIC), and Bayesian information criterion (BIC).
- These metrics are also helpful tools to perform <span style="color: purple;">model selection</span> in GLMs. Additionally, it is essential to highlight that <span style="color: purple;">many</span> GLMs are estimated via <span style="color: purple;">maximum likelihood</span>.

### 1.1. The Crabs Dataset

<center>        
<img src="images/crab.png" width="350" height="350"/>
</center>

- The data frame `crabs` ([Brockmann, 1996](https://ubc.summon.serialssolutions.com/2.0.0/link/0/eLvHCXMwrV3JasMwEBUlpZBLl7Sl6YY_oE4sy5sgFEpICKU9NadcjFYSmtghCyRf0t-tJC_EPhRaepMHS8jSSPM0M3oGALkdx67tCYRyKV0GacCp9CBX60RCySMcYiigy2qpOq_F1ZiMLqL0v-mFYrZvvd4JXXcPEnOUZbU1z6W-fxdoh6eO-XQUvDyGCnXrbK_hxCkDDCHKgs9KH20FelDOR_pzWxXbdYhljTEanoF10e8iC6V2SbDK9Pg_H3gOTnPsar1kynYBjkTSAs1yC923wMkkNaVL8NVbkNXn8wcxjJ8b0euaZysTvyuzVJUYH9i6Kpsl1ijVOSbTtPZ2f6V6nYuectnbbLGdb2tNLNP5fjkVi1J-BcbDwbg_svOfQNhMIRdsu4KHEnIsIiQYJoGQvsKQmAuOsE8lojRnrPEIlZQHHIUEEs8PBVHQjaJr0EjSRNwAS8ebmMNk4DHkRYgQSt2ARoxRnzuhJG2AitmNlxnVR3x4REI41sMf6-GP8-GPd20QmVn7RZV4MB7p0u3fq96BZpY-rn1B96CxWW3FgyGOeDR6_g1rIQSN)) is a dataset detailing the <span style="color: purple;">counts of satellite male crabs</span> residing around a female crab nest.

---

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(glmbb)

data(crabs)
crabs <- crabs |>
  rename(n_males = satell) |>
  dplyr::select(-y)
head(crabs, n = 15)
```

### 1.2. Estimation

<span style="color: purple;">To perform model selection</span>, let us estimate two Poisson regression models with `n_males` as a response:

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\textbf{Model 1:} & \\ 
& h(\lambda_i) = \log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{\texttt{width}_i}. \\
\textbf{Model 2:} & \\ 
& h(\lambda_i) = \log (\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{\texttt{width}_i} + \beta_2 X_{\texttt{color_darker}_i} +  \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \beta_3 X_{\texttt{color_light}_i} + \beta_4 X_{\texttt{color_medium}_i}.
\end{align*}
:::

### Main Statistical Inquiry

- We want to determine which Poisson regression model fits the data better: <span style="color: purple;">Model 1</span> or <span style="color: purple;">Model 2</span>.
- Then, via `glm()` and `crabs`, we obtain our regression estimates.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
poisson_model <- glm(
  formula = n_males ~ width,
  family = poisson, data = crabs
)
poisson_model_2 <- glm(
  formula = n_males ~ width + color,
  family = poisson, data = crabs
)
```

### 1.3. Goodness of Fit Test

::: {.small-text}
- The <span style="color: purple;">deviance</span> ($D_k$) criterion can be used to compare a given model with $k$ regressors with that of a <span style="color: purple;">baseline model</span>.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
> **Heads-up:** The usual <span style="color: purple;">baseline model</span> is the <span style="color: purple;">saturated</span> or <span style="color: purple;">full model</span>, which perfectly fits the data because it allows a distinct Poisson mean $\lambda_i$ for the $i$th observation in the training dataset ($i = 1, \dots, n$), <span style="color: purple;">unrelated to the $k$ regressors</span>.
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text}
- The <span style="color: purple;">maximized likelihood</span> of this full model is denoted as $\hat{\mathscr{l}}_f$. 
- Let $\hat{\mathscr{l}}_k$ be the value of the maximized likelihood computed from our dataset of $n$ observations with $k$ regressors.
:::

#### Comparing the fits

::: {.small-text}

- We can compare the fits provided by these two models by the deviance $D_k$ given by

$$D_k = -2 \log \left( \frac{\hat{\mathscr{l}}_k}{\hat{\mathscr{l}}_f} \right) =  -2 \left[ \log \left( \hat{\mathscr{l}}_k \right) - \log \left( \hat{\mathscr{l}}_f \right) \right].$$

::: incremental
$D_k$ expresses <span style="color: purple;">how much our given model deviates from the full model on log-likelihood scale</span>:

- <span style="color: purple;">Large values</span> of $D_k$ arise when $\hat{\mathscr{l}}_k$ is small relative to $\hat{\mathscr{l}}_f$, indicating that <span style="color: purple;">our given model fits the data poorly compared to the baseline model</span>.
- <span style="color: purple;">Small values</span> of $D_k$ arise when $\hat{\mathscr{l}}_k$ is similar to $\hat{\mathscr{l}}_f$, indicating that <span style="color: purple;">our given model provides a good fit to the data compared to the baseline model</span>.
:::
:::

#### Formula for $D_k$ in Poisson regression

<br>

::: {.small-text}
- <span style="color: purple;">Specifically for Poisson regression with $k$ regressors</span>, it can be shown that $D_k$ is:

\begin{gather}
\hat{\lambda}_i = \exp{\left( \hat{\beta_0} + \hat{\beta}_1 x_{i,1} + \dots + \hat{\beta}_k x_{i,k} \right)} \\
D_k = 2 \sum_{i = 1}^n \left[ y_i \log \left( \frac{y_i}{\hat{\lambda}_i} \right) - \left( y_i - \hat{\lambda}_i \right) \right]
\end{gather}

- Note $y_i$ is the $i$th observed response in the training set of size $n$. 
- When $y_i = 0$ counts, then $\log \left( \frac{y_i}{\hat{\lambda}_i} \right)$ is assumed as $0$.
:::


#### Intuition behind $D_k$

- $D_k$ depicts the agreement of our model with $k$ regressors to the observed data. 
- Hence, it can be used to test the goodness of fit; i.e., <span style="color: purple;">whether our fitted model fits the data better than the saturated model, which makes it correctly specified (with a level of significance $\alpha$!)</span>: 

. . .

\begin{gather*}
H_0: \text{Our}\textbf{ Model with $k$ regressors} \\ \text{ fits the data better than the } \textbf{Saturated Model.} \\
H_a: \text{Otherwise.}
\end{gather*}

#### Testing `poisson_model_2`!

\begin{align*}
\textbf{Model 2:} & \\ 
h(\lambda_i) &= \log (\lambda_i) \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{\texttt{width}_i} + \beta_2 X_{\texttt{color_darker}_i} +  \\ & \qquad \beta_3 X_{\texttt{color_light}_i} + \beta_4 X_{\texttt{color_medium}_i}.
\end{align*}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
summary_poisson_model_2 <- glance(poisson_model_2)
summary_poisson_model_2
```

#### Asymptotic distribution of $D_k$

- Column `deviance` provides $D_k$ (<span style="color: purple;">residual deviance</span>), which is the <span style="color: purple;">test statistic</span>. <span style="color: purple;">Asymptotically</span>, we have the following <span style="color: purple;">null distribution</span>:
$$
D_k \sim \chi^2_{n - (k + 1)}.
$$
- The degrees of freedom (column `df.residual` in our `glance()` output) are the <span style="color: purple;">difference between the training set size $n$ and the number of regression parameters in our model (including the intercept $\beta_0$).</span>

#### Computing $p$-value via `R`

- Let us obtain the corresponding $p\text{-value}$ for this test. We can do it using `pchisq()`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
pchisq(summary_poisson_model_2$deviance,
  df = summary_poisson_model_2$df.residual,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)
```

- We obtain a $p\text{-value} < .001$, which gives statistical evidence to state that our `poisson_model_2` is <span style="color: purple;">not</span> correctly specified when compared to the saturated model.

### 1.4. Analysis of Deviance for Nested Models

::: {.small-text}
- We can use analysis of deviance for model selection when two models are <span style="color: purple;">nested</span>. 
- Hence, we will test our two Poisson models:

\begin{align*}
\textbf{Model 1:} & \\ 
& h(\lambda_i) = \log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{\texttt{width}_i}. \\
\textbf{Model 2:} & \\ 
& h(\lambda_i) = \log (\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{\texttt{width}_i} + \beta_2 X_{\texttt{color_darker}_i} +  \\ & \qquad \qquad \qquad \quad \beta_3 X_{\texttt{color_light}_i} + \beta_4 X_{\texttt{color_medium}_i}.
\end{align*}
:::

#### Hypothesis testing

::: {.small-text}
- This specific model selection will involve a hypothesis testing. The hypotheses are:

\begin{gather*}
H_0: \textbf{Model 1} \text{ fits the data better than } \textbf{Model 2} \\
H_a: \textbf{Model 2} \text{ fits the data better than } \textbf{Model 1}.
\end{gather*}
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
anova(poisson_model, poisson_model_2, test = "Chi")
```

#### Analysis of deviance

<br>

- Let $D_2$ be the deviance (column `Resid. Dev`) for <span style="color: purple;">Model 2</span> (`poisson_model_2`) in row 2 and $D_1$ (column `Resid. Dev`) the deviance for <span style="color: purple;">Model 1</span> (`poisson_model`) in row 1.
- The <span style="color: purple;">test statistic</span> $\Delta_D$ (column `Deviance`) for the analysis of deviance is given by $\Delta_D = D_1 - D_2 \sim \chi^2_{3}$.

. . .

- $\Delta_D$ is <span style="color: purple;">asymptotically</span> (i.e., $n \rightarrow \infty$) is [**Chi-squared distributed**](https://www.math.wm.edu/~leemis/chart/UDR/PDFs/Chisquare.pdf) with $3$ degrees of freedom (column `Df`) under $H_0$ <span style="color: purple;">for this specific case</span>.


#### What is the conclusion?

<br>

- <span style="color: purple;">In the context of model selection</span>, we would choose `poisson_model_2`, that also includes the `color` of the female prosoma.

> **Heads-up:** The degrees of freedom are the <span style="color: purple;">regression parameters of difference between both models</span>. Formally, this nested hypothesis testing is called the <span style="color: purple;">likelihood-ratio test</span>.

### 1.5. Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)

- <span style="color: purple;">Analysis of deviance</span> only allows to test <span style="color: purple;">nested</span> regression models.
- Thus, we need alternatives for model selection. 

. . .

- <span style="color: purple;">AIC makes possible to compare models that are either nested or not.</span> 
- For a model with $k$ terms and a deviance $D_k$, AIC is defined as:
$$
\mbox{AIC}_k = D_k + 2k.
$$

#### What are the AIC rules?

- Models with <span style="color: purple;">smaller</span> values of $\mbox{AIC}_k$ are preferred. 
- That said, $\mbox{AIC}_k$ favours models with small values of $D_k$.

> **Heads-up:** $\mbox{AIC}_k$ penalizes for including more regressors in the model. Hence, it discourages overfitting. This is why we select that model with the smallest $\mbox{AIC}_k$.

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="150" height="150"/>
</center>

#### AIC in `R`!

::: {.small-text}

- The function `glance()` shows us the $\mbox{AIC}_k$ by model.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(poisson_model) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(poisson_model_2) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

> Following the results of the `AIC` column, we choose `poisson_model_2` over `poisson_model`.

:::


### 1.6. Bayesian Information Criterion

- An alternative to AIC is the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). 
- <span style="color: purple;">The BIC also makes possible to compare models that are either nested or not.</span> 

. . .

- For a model with $k$ terms, a deviance $D_k$, and fitted via a training set of size $n$; BIC is defined as:
$$
\mbox{BIC}_k = D_k + k \log (n).
$$

#### What are the BIC rules?

- Models with <span style="color: purple;">smaller</span> values of $\mbox{BIC}_k$ are preferred. 
- That said, $\mbox{BIC}_k$ also favours models with small values of $D_k.$

. . .

> **Heads-up:** The differences between AIC and BIC will be more pronounced in datasets with large sample sizes $n$. As the BIC penalty of $k \log (n)$ will always be larger than the AIC penalty of $2k$ when $n > 7$, <span style="color: purple;">BIC tends to select models with fewer regressors than AIC</span>.

#### BIC in `R`!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(poisson_model) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
glance(poisson_model_2) |> mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

. . .

::: {.small-text-v2}

> Following the results of the `AIC` column, we already chose `poisson_model_2` over `poisson_model`. Nonetheless, the `BIC` is penalizing the `poisson_model_2` for having more model parameters, so `poisson_model` would be chosen under this criterion.

:::

#### What is the statistical rationale behind both metrics?

- **AIC:** From a given set of models (either nested or non-nested) fitted via a common training dataset, this metric aims to select the model with <span style="color: purple;">the best predictive performance</span> even though <span style="color: purple;">this model chosen might not be the true one that generates the training data</span>.

. . .

- **BIC:** From a given set of models (either nested or non-nested) fitted via a common training dataset, this metric will tend to select <span style="color: purple;">the true model that is generating the training data as $n$ approaches infinity</span> and <span style="color: purple;">as long as the true model is within this given set of models</span>. 

## 2. Categorical Type Responses

- Now, we will cover those <span style="color: purple;">discrete responses with more than two categories</span>:

. . .

> <span style="color: purple;">Nominal:</span> We have categories that do not follow any specific order.
>
> <span style="color: purple;">Ordinal:</span> The categories, in this case, follow a specific order.

. . .

- Let us pave the way to two new GLMs to address this matter: <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial and Ordinal Logistic regressions</span>.

## 3. Multinomial Logistic Regression

<br>

> *Let us check the mind map in the lecture notes*

- <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial Logistic regression</span> is a maximum likelihood-based GLM that addresses inferential (and predictive!) inquiries where the response is <span style="color: purple;">categorical</span> and <span style="color: purple;">nominal</span>.

### 3.1. The Spotify Dataset

> *A sub-sample of the Spotify song data originally collected by Kaylin Pavlik (kaylinquest) and distributed through the `R` for Data Science TidyTuesday project.*

<center>        
<img src="https://storage.googleapis.com/pr-newsroom-wp/1/2018/11/Spotify_Logo_CMYK_Green.png" width="540" height="162"/>
</center>

> Copyright © 2025 Spotify AB. Spotify is a registered trademark of the Spotify Group.

#### Let us take a look at the data!

- The `spotify` dataset is a sample of $n = 350$ songs with different variables by column.
- This dataset has 23 variables in total. 
- The $n = 350$ songs belong to 44 different artists.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
spotify <- read_csv(file = 'data/spotify.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)
spotify
```

### iClicker Question

- Having checked the description of the `spotify` dataset, suppose we want to conduct an inferential study. 
- What would be the primary nature of our conclusions?

::: {.small-text}

**A.** We could draw causation conclusions across all music platforms.

**B.** We could draw association conclusions on the Spotify platform.

**C.** We could draw association conclusions across all music platforms.

**D.** We could draw causation conclusions on the Spotify platform.

:::

### Main Statistical Inquiries

- I am <span style="color: purple;">big fan</span> of the electronic dance music (`edm`) catalogue on Spotify. Nevertheless, I do not have access to their whole song database. 

. . .

- Still, I would like to:

  * Statistically quantify how <span style="color: purple;">how danceable</span> `edm` is **compared to other genres on the platform**, and by how much.
  * Statistically quantify <span style="color: purple;">how euphoric</span> `edm` is **compared to other genres on the platform**, and by how much.

### 3.2. Data Wrangling and Summary

- We will extract these <span style="color: purple;">key variables by song</span> from the `spotify` dataset:
  1. `genre`: genre of the playlist where the song belongs (a <span style="color: purple;">categorical</span> and <span style="color: purple;">nominal</span> variable).
  2. `danceability`:  a <span style="color: purple;">numerical</span> score from 0 (not danceable) to 100 (danceable) based on features such as tempo, rhythm, etc.
  3. `valence`: a <span style="color: purple;">numerical</span> score from 0 (the song is more negative, sad, angry) to 100 (the song is more positive, happy, <span style="color: purple;">euphoric</span>).

#### Preparing our training dataset!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
spotify_training <- spotify |>
  select(title, artist, album_name, genre, danceability, valence) |>
  mutate(genre = as.factor(genre))
spotify_training
```


#### Checking all different genres!

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
levels(spotify_training$genre)
```

<br>

> **Heads-up:** Note that factor-type `genre` has six levels (`edm` refers to <span style="color: purple;">electronic dance music</span> and `r&b` to <span style="color: purple;">rhythm and blues</span>). Moreover, <span style="color: purple;">from a coding perspective</span>, `edm` is the <span style="color: purple;">baseline</span> level (it is located on the <span style="color: purple;">left-hand side</span> in the `levels()` output).

#### Creating a dataset summary!

::: {.small-text}

- Let us summarize the data by `genre`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
spotify_training |> tabyl(genre) |>
  adorn_totals("row") |>
  adorn_pct_formatting()
```

- Having checked this `genre` composition, we have an acceptable number of songs to draw inference from. 
- Moreover, an imbalanced classification will be dealt with the <span style="color: purple;">distributional assumption</span> of the Multinomial Logistic regression.

:::

### 3.3. Exploratory Data Analysis

- As done in our previous lecture, let us take a look at the data first. 
- Note that `genre` is a <span style="color: purple;">discrete nominal response</span>. 
- Hence, we could use the following side-by-side plots for both `danceability` and `valence`:
  - <span style="color: purple;">Boxplots.</span>
  - <span style="color: purple;">Violin plots.</span>

#### Plots!

```{r}
#| echo: false
spotify <- read_csv(file = 'data/spotify.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)

genre_danceability_side_boxplots <- spotify |>
  ggplot(aes(genre, danceability)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = genre)) +
  labs(y = "Danceability \n (0-100)", x = "Genre") +
  ggtitle("Side-by-Side Boxplots for Danceability") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 55, angle = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "BuPu")

genre_danceability_side_violin <- spotify |>
  ggplot(aes(genre, danceability)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = genre)) +
  labs(y = "Danceability \n (0-100)", x = "Genre") +
  ggtitle("Side-by-Side Violin Plots for Danceability") +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean, colour = "orange", geom = "point",
    shape = 18, size = 11
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 55, angle = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "BuPu")

genre_valence_side_boxplots <- spotify |>
  ggplot(aes(genre, valence)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = genre)) +
  labs(y = "Valence (0-100)", x = "Genre") +
  ggtitle("Side-by-Side Boxplots for Valence") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 55, angle = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "BuPu")

genre_valence_side_violin <- spotify |>
  ggplot(aes(genre, valence)) +
  geom_violin(aes(fill = genre)) +
  labs(y = "Valence (0-100)", x = "Genre") +
  ggtitle("Side-by-Side Violin Plots for Valence") +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean, colour = "orange", geom = "point",
    shape = 18, size = 11
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 65, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 55, angle = 0),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 55),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "BuPu")
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 45
#| fig.height: 25

plot_grid(genre_danceability_side_boxplots, genre_danceability_side_violin,
  genre_valence_side_boxplots, genre_valence_side_violin,
  nrow = 2
)
```

### 3.4. Data Modelling Framework

- A <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial Logistic Regression model</span> is a suitable approach to our statistical inquiries given that `genre` is <span style="color: purple;">categorical</span> and <span style="color: purple;">nominal</span> (our response of interest) subject to the <span style="color: purple;">numerical</span> regressors `danceability` and `valence`. 
- Moreover, its corresponding regression estimates will allow us <span style="color: purple;">to measure variable association</span>.

<center>        
<img src="images/panda.png" width="200" height="200"/>
</center>

#### 3.4.1. Primary Intuition of the Multinomial Logistic Regression Model

- Digging into the Multinomial regression model will require checking <span style="color: purple;">Binary Logistic regression</span> first. 
- Thus, suppose we are initially interested in two genres: `edm` and `latin`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
bin_spotify_training <- spotify_training |> filter(genre %in% c("edm", "latin")) |> mutate(genre = droplevels(genre))
head(bin_spotify_training, n = 3)
```

#### A note on the baseline level!

<br>

- `edm` is the baseline level (i.e., it appears on the left-hand side in the `levels()` output).

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
levels(bin_spotify_training$genre)
```


#### Reminder on Binary Logistic Modelling

<br>

- Assuming we have a <span style="color: purple;">training set</span> of $n$ elements, recall that the $i$th response (for $i = 1, \dots, n$) in a <span style="color: purple;">Binary Logistic regression</span> is 

$$
Y_i =
\begin{cases}
1 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if the genre is } \texttt{latin},\\
0 \; \; \; \; \mbox{if the baseline genre is } \texttt{edm}.
\end{cases}
$$

- Therefore, $Y_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i)$, whose probability of success is $p_i$.


#### Link Function in Binary Logistic Regression

- We will use the following <span style="color: purple;">link function</span> (where $X_{i,\texttt{dance}}$ and $X_{i,\texttt{val}}$ are the `danceability` and `valence` scores for the $i$th song, respectively):

\begin{align*}
\mbox{logit}(p_i) &= \log\left(\frac{p_i}{1 - p_i}\right) \nonumber \\
&= \log \left[ \frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{latin}\mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}) \right] \nonumber \\
&= \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i,\texttt{dance}} + \beta_2 X_{i,\texttt{val}}.
\end{align*}


#### Binary Logistic Regression Estimation via `R`

- Recall that this model can be fitted as follows:

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
spotify_bin_log_model <- glm(formula = genre ~ danceability + valence,
  data = bin_spotify_training,
  family = binomial
)
```


#### Inference in Binary Logistic Regression

- Note that only `valence` is statistically significant for the response `genre` ($p\text{-value} < .01$).

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
tidy(spotify_bin_log_model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

#### Coefficient Interpretation in Binary Logistic Regression

- Then, we make the corresponding coefficient interpretations (the previous output already provides the estimate on the odds scale via `exponentiate = TRUE`):

<br>

> For each unit increase in the `valence` score in the Spotify catalogue, the song is 1.05 times more probable to be `latin` than `edm`.

#### 3.4.2.  More than One Logit Function

::: {.small-text-v2}

> <span style="color: purple;">What if our response is nominal and has more than two categories?</span> 

- In that case, let us suppose that a given <span style="color: purple;">discrete nominal response $Y_i$ has categories $1, 2, \dots, m$</span>.

> **Heads-up:** Categories $1, 2, \dots, m$ <span style="color: purple;">are merely labels here</span>. Thus, they <span style="color: purple;">do not</span> implicate an ordinal scale.

- This regression approach assumes a [**Multinomial distribution**](https://stats.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Probability_Theory/Probability_Mathematical_Statistics_and_Stochastic_Processes_(Siegrist)/11%3A_Bernoulli_Trials/11.05%3A_The_Multinomial_Distribution) where $p_{i,1}, p_{i,2}, \dots, p_{i,m}$ are the probabilities that $Y_i$ will belong to categories $1, 2, \dots, m$ respectively; i.e.,

$$
P(Y_i = 1) = p_{i,1} \;\;\;\; P(Y_i = 2) = p_{i,2} \;\; \dots \;\; P(Y_i = m) = p_{i,m} \quad \text{where}
$$


$$
\sum_{j = 1}^m p_{i,j} = p_{i,1} + p_{i,2} + \dots + p_{i,m} = 1.
$$
:::


#### Is one logarithm of the odds enough?

- The Multinomial Logistic regression <span style="color: purple;">also models the logarithm of the odds</span>. 
- However, only one logarithm of the odds (or <span style="color: purple;">logit</span>) will not be enough anymore. 

. . .

- Here is what we can do:
  1. Pick one of the categories to be the <span style="color: purple;">baseline</span>. For example, the category "$1$" (or `edm` in our context).
  2. For each of the <span style="color: purple;">other</span> categories, we model the logarithm of the odds to the baseline category.

#### Checking response levels!

- Let us set the Multinomial Logistic regression model with `genre` as a response subject to `danceability` and `valence` as continuous regressors. 
- Level `edm` will be the baseline:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
levels(spotify_training$genre)
```


#### Log-odds and odds ratio

<br>

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{latin} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}\right] \\ 
&= \beta_0^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})} + \beta_1^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{dance}} + \beta_2^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{val}}
\end{align*}
:::

<br>

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{latin}\mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})} &= \exp\left[\beta_0^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\right] \times \exp\left[\beta_1^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{dance}}\right] \times \\
& \qquad \exp\left[\beta_2^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{val}}\right]
\end{align*}
:::


#### Probability

<br>

::: {.small-text-v2}
\begin{gather*}
p_{i,\texttt{edm}} = P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}}) = \\ 
\frac{1}{1 + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)}
\end{gather*}
:::

#### Similarly ...

<br>

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{pop} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}\right] \\
&= \beta_0^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})} + \beta_1^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{dance}} + \beta_2^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{val}} \\
\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{r&b} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}\right] \\ 
&= \beta_0^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})} + \beta_1^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{dance}} + \beta_2^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{val}} \\
\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{rap} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}\right] \\
&= \beta_0^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})} + \beta_1^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{dance}} + \beta_2^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{val}}
\end{align*}
:::

#### Similarly (cont’d)

<br>

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})} &= \log\left[\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{rock} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i, \texttt{dance}}, X_{i, \texttt{val}})}\right] \\ 
&= \beta_0^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})} + \beta_1^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{dance}} + \beta_2^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})} X_{i, \texttt{val}}.
\end{align*}
:::

#### Odds

<br>

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{pop}\mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}& = \exp\left[\beta_0^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\right] \times \exp\left[\beta_1^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{dance}}\right] \times \\ & \qquad \exp\left[\beta_2^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{val}}\right] \\
\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{r&b}\mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})} &= \exp\left[\beta_0^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\right] \times \exp\left[\beta_1^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{dance}}\right] \times \\
& \qquad \exp\left[\beta_2^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{val}}\right]
\end{align*}
:::

#### Odds (cont’d)

<br>

::: {.small-text}
\begin{align*}
\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{rap}\mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})} &=  \exp\left[\beta_0^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\right] \times \exp\left[\beta_1^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{dance}}\right] \times \\ 
& \qquad \exp\left[\beta_2^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{val}}\right] \\
\frac{P(Y_i = \texttt{rock}\mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})}{P(Y_i = \texttt{edm} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}})} &= \exp\left[\beta_0^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\right] \times \exp\left[\beta_1^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{dance}}\right] \times \\
& \qquad \exp\left[\beta_2^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})} X_{i,\texttt{val}}\right].
\end{align*}
:::

#### Probabilities

::: {.small-text-v2}
\begin{gather*}
p_{i,\texttt{latin}} = P(Y_i = \texttt{latin} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}}) = \\ \frac{\exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big)}{1 + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)} \\
p_{i,\texttt{pop}} = P(Y_i = \texttt{pop} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}}) = \\ \frac{\exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big)}{1 + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)}
\end{gather*}
:::

. . .

::: {.small-text-v2}
\begin{gather*}
p_{i,\texttt{r&b}} = P(Y_i = \texttt{r&b} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}}) = \\ \frac{\exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big)}{1 + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)} \\
p_{i,\texttt{rap}} = P(Y_i = \texttt{rap} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}}) = \\ \frac{\exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big)}{1 + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)}
\end{gather*}
:::

#### Probabilities (cont’d)

<br>

::: {.small-text-v2}
\begin{gather*}
p_{i,\texttt{rock}} = P(Y_i = \texttt{rock} \mid X_{i,\texttt{dance}}, X_{i,\texttt{val}}) = \\ \frac{\exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)}{1 + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{pop},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rap},\texttt{edm})}\big) + \exp\big(\eta_i^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}\big)}.
\end{gather*}
:::

### iClicker Question

- Answer **TRUE** or **FALSE**:

> Now that we removed the restriction of only one link function, we also removed the distributional assumption for $Y_i$. Hence, our model has no distributional assumption.

**A.** TRUE

**B.** FALSE

### iClicker Question

- Answer **TRUE** or **FALSE**:

> From the statistical point of view, the model is now non-parametric.

**A.** TRUE

**B.** FALSE

### 3.5. Estimation

- To fit the model with the package `nnet`, we use the function `multinom()`, which obtains the corresponding estimates. 
- The estimates are obtained through <span style="color: purple;">maximum likelihood</span>, where we assume a <span style="color: purple;">Multinomial joint probability mass function</span> of the $n$ responses $Y_i$.

#### The code!

<br>

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
spotify_mult_log_model <- multinom(
  formula = genre ~ danceability + valence,
  data = spotify_training
)
```

### 3.6. Inference

- We also use the <span style="color: purple;">Wald statistic</span> $z_j^{(u, v)} = \frac{\hat{\beta}_j^{(u, v)}}{\mbox{se}\left(\hat{\beta}_j^{(u, v)}\right)}$ to test the hypotheses
\begin{gather*}
H_0: \beta_j^{(u, v)} = 0\\
H_a: \beta_j^{(u, v)} \neq 0.
\end{gather*}

. . .

- Provided the sample size $n$ is large enough, $z_j$ has an <span style="color: purple;">approximately Standard Normal distribution</span> under $H_0$.

#### Confidence Intervals (CIs) for Odds

- We can also use the function `tidy()` from the `broom` package along with argument `conf.int = TRUE` to get the 95% CIs <span style="color: purple;">by default</span>.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
mult_output <- tidy(spotify_mult_log_model, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE)
mult_output |>
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round, 3)
```

#### Filtering those significant estimates...

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
mult_output |>
  dplyr::filter(p.value < 0.05)
```

#### What can we conclude?

<br>

- Since our baseline response is `edm`, we can conclude the following with $\alpha = 0.05$ <span style="color: purple;">on the Spotify platform</span>:
  - There is a statistical difference in `danceability` in `edm` versus `r&b` and `rock`.
  - There is a statistical difference in `valence` in `edm` versus `latin`.

### 3.7. Coefficient Interpretation

:::{.small-text}
> $\beta_2^{(\texttt{latin},\texttt{edm})}$: for each unit increase in the `valence` score in the Spotify catalogue, the song is $1.05$ times more likely to be `latin` than `edm`.

> $\beta_1^{(\texttt{r&b},\texttt{edm})}$: for each unit increase in the `danceability` score in the Spotify catalogue, the odds for a song for being `r&b` decrease by $(1 - 0.963) \times 100\% = 3.7\%$ compared to `edm`.

> $\beta_1^{(\texttt{rock},\texttt{edm})}$: for each unit increase in the `danceability` score in the Spotify catalogue, the odds for a song for being `rock` decrease by $(1 - 0.918) \times 100\% = 8.2\%$ compared to `edm`.
:::

### 3.8. Predictions

- Suppose we want to predict the genre probabilities for a given song with a `danceability` score of `27.5` and `valence` of `30`. 

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
pred_probs <- round(predict(spotify_mult_log_model, tibble(danceability = 27.5, valence = 30), type = "probs"), 2)
pred_probs
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
sum(pred_probs) # Due to rounding, sum is 0.99 and not 1.
```

### 3.9. Model Selection

- <span style="color: purple;">To perform model selection</span>, we can use the same techniques from the Binary Logistic regression model. 
- That said, some `R` coding functions might not be entirely available for the `multinom()` models. 
- Still, these statistical techniques and metrics can be manually coded.
